content: Surgical wounds that become infected are often treated with debridement, a process where necrotic or infected tissue is removed to promote wound healing. Clinicians believe that this intervention can expedite the healing process. However, there is no consensus on which debridement method is most effective for surgical wounds. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various debridement methods on the speed of debridement and the healing of surgical wounds. A comprehensive search was conducted in October 2021 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL. Additional studies were identified through clinical trial registries, reference lists of relevant studies, reviews, meta-analyses, and health technology reports. There were no restrictions on language, publication date, or study setting. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving patients with surgical wounds requiring debridement. These studies reported outcomes such as time to complete wound debridement, time to wound healing, or both. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias using the RoB 1 tool, extracted data, and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. In this fourth update of the review, one additional study was included, bringing the total to six studies with 265 participants aged between 3 and 91 years. Five of these studies were published between 1979 and 1990, and one was published in 2014. The studies were conducted in hospital settings in China, Denmark, Belgium, and the UK. Due to the heterogeneity of the studies, meta-analyses were not feasible. The six studies provided six different comparisons. Four studies evaluated dextranomer beads or paste (autolytic debridement) against different comparators, including Eusol-soaked dressings, 10% aqueous polyvinylpyrrolidone, 0.1% chloramine-soaked dressings, and silicone foam elastomer dressings. One study compared enzymatic debridement using streptokinase/streptodornase with saline-soaked dressings. Another study compared endoscopic surgical debridement with conventional open surgical debridement. Five studies reported the time to complete debridement (defined as achieving a clean wound bed), and three studies reported the time to complete wound healing. Only one study provided effect estimates for time to a clean wound bed and time to complete healing (endoscopic versus open surgical debridement). Another study allowed calculation of effect estimates for time to complete healing (dextranomer paste versus silicone foam elastomer). For the remaining four studies, it was not possible to calculate these outcomes due to missing variance data and participant exclusions. None of the included studies reported outcomes such as the proportion of wounds completely healed, the rate of wound size reduction, the rate of infection, or quality of life. All studies had an unclear or high risk of bias in at least one key domain. Dextranomer paste/beads compared with four different comparators: Four studies compared dextranomer paste or beads with Eusol-soaked gauze (20 participants), 10% aqueous polyvinylpyrrolidone (40 participants), 0.1% chloramine-soaked dressings (28 participants), or silicone foam elastomer (50 participants). There is very low-certainty evidence suggesting no clear difference in time to a clean wound bed between dextranomer beads and Eusol gauze. Adverse events were not reported. There is very low-certainty evidence suggesting no difference in time to a clean wound bed between dextranomer paste and 10% aqueous polyvinylpyrrolidone gauze. Low-certainty evidence suggests no difference in deaths or serious adverse events. There may be a difference in time to a clean wound bed and time to complete healing favoring 0.1% chloramine over dextranomer paste, but the certainty of this evidence is very low. Low-certainty evidence suggests no difference in deaths or serious adverse events. There is very low-certainty evidence suggesting no difference in time to complete healing between dextranomer beads and silicone foam elastomer. Adverse events were not reported. Streptokinase/streptodornase solution compared with saline-soaked dressings: One study (21 participants) compared enzymatic debridement with saline-soaked dressings. Low-certainty evidence suggests no difference in time to a clean wound bed or secondary suture between streptokinase/streptodornase and saline-soaked dressings. Very low-certainty evidence suggests no difference in deaths or serious adverse events. Endoscopic surgical debridement compared with open surgical debridement: One study (106 participants) reported on time to complete wound healing and time to a clean wound bed. Low-certainty evidence suggests that endoscopic surgical debridement may reduce the time to complete wound healing compared to open surgical debridement. Very low-certainty evidence suggests no difference in time to a clean wound bed between the two methods. Adverse events were not reported. Overall, the evidence for all outcomes was of low to very low certainty. Five of the included studies were published before 1991 and investigated treatments that are no longer widely available. For example, dextranomer products are no longer produced globally, except for dextranomer paste, which is only available in South Africa. Eusol, used in one study as a comparator, is rarely used due to its potential harmful effects on healthy tissue. The enzymatic agent streptokinase/streptodornase is no longer available worldwide. Authors' conclusions: The evidence regarding the effects of different debridement methods on complete wound debridement and healing of surgical wounds remains unclear. There is a need for adequately powered, methodologically robust RCTs evaluating contemporary debridement interventions to guide clinical decision-making.
